sents: I'm Kohei, and this is one pricing engine applied to two markets.
Week 1: a developed market with 2.4 million policy rows. Rank 3 of 54.
Week 2: an emerging market with only 2 years of data, and a test book that is 76% new business. Our final file scored 0.1646 on the public leaderboard.
The approach: keep what transfers from the developed market, re-measure what does not, and test every step in both directions.
And AI works alongside me throughout: I used Claude Code, steered from my phone by voice, to explore the data, write and test code, run experiments, and verify its own work.
scenes.oneliner: One engine, two markets: keep what transfers, re-measure the rest, test both ways.

sents: So what changed in the new market?
Motor claims are 34% more frequent, but 42% cheaper.
Glass, third-party and injury claims are far more frequent. Escape of water is far less.
And 3 out of 4 test policies are brand-new customers with no history.
We measured that these differences are stable across both years, instead of assuming it.
scenes.oneliner: The new market differs by peril and by customer mix, not by one level factor.

sents: The method keeps what transfers, and re-measures what does not.
A developed-market model, trained on the variables both markets share, ranks who is risky. I add last year's claim history.
An ensemble of 5 tree models, 7 neural nets and 4 Tweedie models averages out the noise.
Then the emerging book sets the level: claim counts and winsorised severities for each peril, credibility-weighted, plus one gender factor.
The emerging data decides how much. The developed data decides who.
scenes.oneliner: The developed market decides who is risky; the emerging book decides how much.
Final submission: 16 models in three groups, averaged, then calibrated to the emerging book.
sents: Here is the structure of the final submission.
5 tree models: LightGBM with 4 and 8 leaves, single and 3-seed fits, a column-sampled variant, and an XGBoost model.
7 neural nets: TabM, TabM with piecewise-linear encoding, and TabM with quantile inputs, each as a single and a 3-seed fit, plus one wider TabM.
4 direct Tweedie models complete it, at 4 and 8 leaves, single and 3-seed.
Each group is averaged with equal weights: trees and nets 37.5% each, Tweedie 25%. Then the emerging level and the gender factor are applied.
With 2 years of data, a single split can mistake noise for signal.
So every change is tested in both directions, calibrating on 2023 and scoring 2024 and the reverse, and kept only if neither gets worse.
That took the score from 0.1110, for an emerging-only model, to 0.1405.
More than 30 ideas were rejected this way, including pooled training and a GLM blend.
A simulation with a known truth confirmed the level method, and a ceiling analysis showed that a perfect level is worth at most 0.005.
scenes.oneliner: Every change is kept only if it improves the score in both time directions.

sents: Here is how that looked in practice.
Claude Code explored both markets, wrote the code with 125 tests, and ran the experiments, while more than 10 helper sessions refit models in parallel.
A blind second agent compared the markets from the raw tables alone.
And verification caught real errors: unsupported statements in a first draft, a simulator bug that looked like a model bias, and a net that Part 1 had already rejected.
Every number traces to a command.
scenes.oneliner: AI does the legwork; verification and decisions stay with me, and are recorded.

sents: One example of how this changes the way I work.
Part of Week 2 was done from my phone, on a bus, with no laptop. Claude Code ran in the cloud, and I controlled it remotely from the Claude app.
I gave my instructions by voice. The app transcribes my speech, Claude Code picks it up, runs the work, and reports back while I am on the move.
That is AI-assisted actuarial work, away from the desk.
scenes.oneliner: Example: Claude Code, remote-controlled from my phone by voice, on a bus.

sents: Guardrails: a leak alarm, reproducibility checks, a model card, and 84 recorded decisions.
The biggest uncertainty is the buildings level. Plus or minus 20% is about 0.01 of D².
And gender rating is flagged for regulatory review.
Built with an AI teammate, from a bus seat. Thank you.
scenes.oneliner: Guardrails and stated limits: what could go wrong, and how we would notice.
